blocks.text: “Don't say yes,” Miss Smallweed replies, “because I know what you girls are. Do it without saying it, and then I may begin to believe you.”

Charley swallows a big mouthful of tea to show that she obeys. She also breaks up the Druidical ruins so much that Miss Smallweed orders her not to eat greedily. Doing that, Miss Smallweed remarks, is disgusting “in you girls.” Just then, there is a knock at the door. Without it, Charley might have some more difficulty satisfying her ideas about girls in general.
“See who it is, and don't chew when you open it!” cries Judy.

The object of her attention goes out to do this. Miss Smallweed uses that chance to mix the rest of the bread and butter together into a messy pile. She also sends two or three dirty tea-cups out into the low tide of the bowl of tea. This is a hint that she considers the eating and drinking finished.
“Now! Who is it, and what's wanted?” Judy says in her sharp, irritable way.
It seems to be someone called “Mr. George.” Without any other introduction or polite ceremony, Mr. George walks in.
“Whew!” says Mr. George. “You are hot here. Always a fire, eh? Well! Perhaps you are right to get used to one.” Mr. George says this last part to himself as he nods to Grandfather Smallweed.
“Ho! It's you!” cries the old gentleman. “How do you do? How do you do?”
“Not too good, not too bad,” replies Mr. George, sitting down on a chair. “I have had the honor of seeing your granddaughter before. My respects to you, miss.”
“This is my grandson,” says Grandfather Smallweed. “You haven't seen him before. He works in the law, and he is not at home much.”

“My respects to him, too! He is like his sister. He is very like his sister. He is devilish like his sister,” says Mr. George. He puts strong stress on the word “devilish,” and not completely as a compliment.
“And how does the world treat you, Mr. George?” Grandfather Smallweed asks, slowly rubbing his legs.
“Pretty much as usual. Like a football.”

He is a fifty-year-old man with dark, tanned skin. He is well-built and good-looking, with closely curled dark hair, bright eyes, and a broad chest. His tough, muscular, and powerful hands are as sunburnt as his face. Clearly, they have been used to quite a rough life. One unusual thing about him is that he sits forward on his chair. He sits as if, from long habit, he is leaving space for some clothing or equipment that he has completely put aside. His step is also steady, regular, and heavy. It would go well with the heavy clash and ringing sound of spurs. He is closely shaved now. Still, he holds his mouth as if there had been a big moustache on his upper lip for years. Sometimes he also puts the open palm of his wide brown hand upon it, and this habit gives the same impression. All in all, someone might guess that Mr. George had once been a cavalry soldier.

Mr. George makes a remarkable contrast to the Smallweed family. No cavalry soldier was ever assigned to stay with a household more unlike himself. It is like comparing a wide-bladed sword to a knife for opening oysters. He has a strong, fully grown body, while they have small, poorly grown bodies. His big, open manner fills any amount of space, while they have small, narrow, cramped ways. His strong, ringing voice also contrasts with their sharp, thin voices. All these things are complete opposites in the strongest and strangest way. He sits in the middle of the cheerless parlor, leaning a little forward. His hands are on his thighs, and his elbows are held out wide. He looks as if he would absorb the whole family into himself if he stayed there long, together with the whole four-roomed house and even the extra little back-kitchen.
“Do you rub your legs to rub life into them?” he asks Grandfather Smallweed, after looking around the room.
“Well, it's partly a habit, Mr. George, and—yes—it partly helps the blood flow,” he replies.
